name: Gangotri Dham–Lakhnadon Highway
aka: Formed mainly from stretches of the former NH 108, NH 94, NH 58, NH 119, NH 91 and NH 86
agency: NHAI; Border Roads Organisation on the Himalayan section

timeline.event: Char Dham road project launched, widening the Rishikesh–Gangotri stretch of the highway
The 440 m Chamba tunnel, dug by the Border Roads Organisation under Chamba town, is holed through and completed

history: NH 34 starts high in the Himalayas at Gangotri Dham, one of the four Char Dham pilgrimage shrines, and follows the Bhagirathi — the young Ganga — down through Uttarkashi to Rishikesh and Haridwar. It then crosses the plains of western Uttar Pradesh through Meerut, Aligarh and Kanpur, drops into the dry Bundelkhand country around Hamirpur and Mahoba, and climbs into central Madhya Pradesh past Chhatarpur, Damoh and Jabalpur. The route was pieced together in the 2010s renumbering by joining several older highways, among them the old NH 108, NH 94, NH 58, NH 119, NH 91 and NH 86. Its mountain section is one of the roads being widened under the Char Dham Pariyojana, launched in 2016 to give the four shrines all-weather access, and in 2020 the Border Roads Organisation completed a 440 m tunnel beneath the crowded hill town of Chamba to clear a long-standing bottleneck. The highway finally ends at Lakhnadon in Madhya Pradesh, where it joins NH 44.
facts: At about 1,426 km, it links a Himalayan shrine with the centre of India.
Its mountain stretch from Rishikesh up to Gangotri is part of the Char Dham pilgrimage road network.
Gangotri, where it begins, sits high in the Himalayas and is cut off by snow for roughly half the year.
Haridwar, one of the holiest cities on the Ganga, sits on its route.
The 440 m Chamba tunnel, completed in 2020, runs right underneath a hill town on the pilgrim road.
It meets NH 35 at Kabrai in Bundelkhand, a town known for its stone quarries.
It ends at Lakhnadon on NH 44, India's longest national highway.
Most of the highway is a two-lane road.
significance: For half the year the top of NH 34 is a pilgrim road: it is how most people reach Gangotri, one of the four Char Dham shrines, and how food and building materials reach the villages of the upper Bhagirathi valley. Lower down it is a plain, hard-working highway tying western Uttar Pradesh, Kanpur, Bundelkhand and central Madhya Pradesh together — a north–south line well away from the big expressway corridors.

engineering.name: Chamba tunnel
engineering.note: 440 m long, dug by the Border Roads Organisation right under the hill town of Chamba and completed in 2020 as part of the Char Dham project; it cuts the crawl through the town from about half an hour to ten minutes

engineering.name: Bhagirathi valley road above Uttarkashi
engineering.note: cut into steep, loose slopes above the river; landslides can shut it for hours during the monsoon

travelNotes: The Gangotri road is open only from about late April, when the shrine opens, until Diwali time in October or November; snow shuts it for the rest of the year, and pilgrims are asked to register before travelling. Between July and September landslides in the Bhagirathi valley can hold traffic for hours. The plains stretch through Meerut, Aligarh and Kanpur is slow and crowded, with thick fog in December and January. Hardly anyone drives the whole route — it is used in sections.
futureUpgrades: The Rishikesh–Gangotri mountain stretch is still being widened and made all-weather under the Char Dham Pariyojana.
